activity_context.topic_title: Calculating Limits of Radical Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

feedback.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{x}-2}{x-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{4}-2}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{x}-2}{x-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-2)(\sqrt{x}+2)}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{x-4}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
